title: Bitwise and Shift Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of bitwise and shift operators in C#.
Identify the relevant operand types, evaluation rules and result types.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integral values. AND (&) keeps a bit set only when both corresponding bits are set; OR (|) sets a bit when either is set; XOR (^) sets a bit when they differ; complement (~) flips every bit. Left shift (<<) moves bits toward higher positions and right shift (>>) moves them toward lower positions. C# also supports unsigned right shift (>>>) for integral types. Shift counts are masked according to the left operand's width; shifts are not a substitute for checked multiplication.
understand.whyItMatters: Bitwise operations are useful for flags, compact protocol fields, masks and low-level data manipulation.
understand.analogy: Imagine each bit as an on/off switch; bitwise operators combine corresponding switches.
understand.analogyLimit: Bitwise operations are easy to misuse and reduce readability when applied without a clear bit layout. Signed right shift and unsigned right shift differ for negative values.

explain.narrative:
## Bitwise logic

For integral operands, `&`, `|` and `^` operate on each corresponding bit. `~` complements every bit. These operators are often used with masks to test, set, clear or toggle flags.

## Shifts

`<<` shifts bits left and fills newly vacated low-order bits with zeros. `>>` is an arithmetic right shift for signed integral types, preserving the sign bit. `>>>` is an unsigned right shift and fills high-order positions with zeros. Shift counts are masked to the width of the left operand (five low bits for 32-bit values and six for 64-bit values).

## Use masks deliberately

Use named constants for flags and masks, and document the bit layout. A shift can discard bits; it is not a general checked multiplication operation.

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.
